title: Decision-Theoretic Approaches for Improved Learning-Augmented Algorithms
claim: Within a family of equally robust algorithms, performance varies sharply with prediction error, and none matches the ideal curve everywhere.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, bold ideal curve, legend overlay at lower right
description: A single line plot with ski season length on the x-axis and performance ratio on the y-axis. The y-axis has symbolic ticks (1, r/(r-1), 2, (2r-1)/(r-1), r-1, r), and the x-axis has symbolic ticks (b/(r-1), b, br/(r-1), b(r-1)). Six thin colored curves show r-robust algorithms with different threshold values T. Each has its own shape. One is a spike followed by a decay. Others are step functions or a linear ramp that ends in a jump to r. A thick black curve marks the ideal performance ratio. It sits at 1, rises, then stays flat just above 1. A legend box in the lower right lists the thresholds. Gray grid lines run behind the curves. The eye goes first to the tall blue spike at the left and the bold black baseline.
caption: Performance functions of $r$-robust algorithms for different threshold values. The curve in bold depicts the ideal performance ratio.
abstract: We initiate the systematic study of decision-theoretic metrics in the design and analysis of algorithms with machine-learned predictions. We introduce approaches based on both deterministic measures such as distance-based evaluation, that help us quantify how close the algorithm is to an ideal solution, and stochastic measures that balance the trade-off between the algorithm's performance and the risk associated with the imperfect oracle. These approaches allow us to quantify the algorithm's performance across the full spectrum of the prediction error, and thus choose the best algorithm within an entire class of otherwise incomparable ones. We apply our framework to three well-known problems from online decision making, namely ski-rental, one-max search, and contract scheduling.
